az_yarba.blurb: YARBA is a compact crag on the lower stretch of the Catalina Highway on Mount Lemmon near Tucson, a short way before the Wall of the Flying Scorpions. It holds five bolted sport lines, all steep, rising roughly 35 feet, with grades from 5.10 into the 5.11 range. The wall faces northwest and gets shade in the morning; it sees no winter sun, while spring and fall are warmer in the afternoon. The name stands for Yet Another Roped Bouldering Area, which fits the short, powerful style. The surrounding Lower Highway crags sit in saguaro desert foothills.

az_cemetery_the_2.blurb: The Cemetery is a small crag on West Twin Butte above the Sedona Cemetery, on the part of Twin Butte best known for sport climbing. Five routes are catalogued, four sport and one trad, with grades from 5.9 up to the 5.12 range and a cluster around 5.10. The centrepiece is a long two-pitch bolted line up the middle of the main buttress, so carry plenty of draws and two ropes for the full length. Getting to the base means a short trail through brush, then a scramble, about ten minutes in total.

az_talon_s_grip_area.blurb: Talon's Grip Area is a small cluster of five routes on the central, west-facing stretch of Raptor Ridge, in Lower Devil's Canyon off Queen Creek Canyon, at roughly 4,000 feet. Three are sport and two are trad. The grades split into two easy 5.8s and a 5.9 at the bottom end, then a 5.11 and a 5.12 for stronger climbers, with nothing in between. That mix gives a mixed party some options, though the harder pair are the draw for sport climbers.

az_quartzite_spring_boulder.blurb: Quartzite Spring Boulder is a single boulder in the Rappel Rock bouldering cluster near the summit of Mount Lemmon, at about 8,800 feet. Its main face is sheer and overhanging, and it looks small from the trail but feels tall once you stand beneath it. Five problems range from V2 up to V11, with a couple of mid-grade lines and a pair of very hard ones at the top end. Part of the landing is angled slab, so bring extra pads plus cord to fix them in place. The boulder sits southwest of a piped spring beside Mt. Lemmon Trail #5.
